new_statements.quote: Even though zam is a monosyllabic language, there are disyllabic morphologically complex words that reveal an iambic stress pattern. The stressed syllable is always heavy while unstressed syllables are always light (Sicoli 2007; Arellanes 2021, among others). [...] The prosodic requirement that the minimal word be a bimoraic foot, even when it is a monosyllable, is because a stressed syllable is bimoraic and a prosodic word must have a stressed syllable. Table 3 shows the words [kàː] 'to move' and [níː] 'foot' in isolation, and finally the compound [kàníː] 'to dance'. The compound word is formed by an unbalanced iambic foot, a canonical iamb according to Hayes (1995).

new_statements.rule_in_words: The lexicon is overwhelmingly monosyllabic, and every prosodic word has exactly one stressed, obligatorily bimoraic (heavy) syllable. In the disyllabic words that exist (compounds, recent loans, morphologically complex forms) stress is iambic: it falls on the last syllable of the base (the final root), and every preceding syllable is light and unstressed. Hernández Luna 2021: 17 states the same rule directionally: 'el acento siempre caerá en la sílaba del borde derecho de la base'. Main acoustic cue is rhyme duration (p. 31), not vowel duration or intensity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; one prominent syllable per prosodic word (culminative bimoraicity, Hernández Luna 2021: 16-17).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Words longer than one syllable are said to be recent loans or morphologically complex; loans adopt the iambic pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prosodic word = base plus preceding pretonic syllables; enclitics are light and outside the stressed domain, and the clitic group has separate tonal effects, p. 21-22). Citation forms are mostly bimoraic monosyllables, so the pattern is only visible in compounds and loans; correlates measured instrumentally on CVCV words (Tables 4-6). Described for Santo Domingo de Morelos speakers (fieldwork 2008-2019, three speakers), not for Cuixtla or Xitla.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes the Santo Domingo de Morelos (Pochutla district) variety, which its authors label "Miahuatec (ISO zam)" (Hernández Luna & Herrera Zendejas 2024: 3). Hernández Luna's 2019 COLMEX thesis (p. 16) states that "el miahuateco propiamente dicho" is one language spoken from the Miahuatlán valley "en municipios como Xitla, Cuixtla y Yogovana" through the sierra to the coast "en municipios como San Agustín Loxicha y Santo Domingo de Morelos", and (p. 18) that Ethnologue splits these communities "sin criterios claros" into Loxicha [ztp], Miahuatlán [zam] and Ozolotepec [zao] Zapotec. Glottolog does not list Santo Domingo de Morelos anywhere; Beam de Azcona (2004: 12) calls it the "same language as San Agustín Loxicha", i.e. Glottolog loxi1235 [ztp]. So by the specialist's own coding this is a zam statement, but by Glottolog/Beam de Azcona it belongs to loxi1235 — and the same 2024 article is already the deciding source in the catalog's loxi1235 record. Treat as one description used for two glottocodes (merge/double-count decision for the catalog). No stress statement exists for the Cuixtla or Xitla towns themselves: Ruegsegger 1955 (Cuixtla) is a wordlist with no stress remark, Ruegsegger 1954 is unpublished, and the 2019 thesis elicited wordlists in Xitla (p. 38) but analyses only SDM, San Agustín Mixtepec and San Bartolo Yautepec.
